claim: ImmunoCluster identified three populations of Tregs: Tregs (CD25+CD127low) (3.6%, 1.3–5.5), Treg A (CD25+CD127low CD45RA+) (0.7%, 0.1–2.0), and Treg B-cells (CD25+CD127lowCCR4+CD95high) (0.9%, 0.2–2.4).
source: Additionally, three populations of Tregs were identified by the ImmunoCluster tool: Tregs (CD25+CD127low) (3.6%, 1.3–5.5), Treg A (CD25+CD127low CD45RA+) (0.7%, 0.1–2.0), and Treg B-cells (CD25+CD127lowCCR4+CD95high) (0.9%, 0.2–2.4) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the FC analysis, supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The distribution of Treg A and B in healthy donors was as expected.
source: The abundance of Treg A and B for all HDs is shown in Figure 6D, and their distribution was as expected (Kordasti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the FC analysis that matches expectations from Kordasti et al., 2016, supported by Figure 6D.

claim: ImmunoCluster is an open-access easy-to-use framework for LMC, IMC, and FC dataset analyses.
source: Here, we provide an overview of the flexibility and scope for utilizing ImmunoCluster, an open-access easy-to-use framework for LMC, IMC, and FC dataset analyses.
evidence: This is a summary statement about ImmunoCluster.

claim: The purpose for creating the ImmunoCluster framework was to support nonspecialist researchers to carry out complex immunophenotyping experiments.
source: The purpose for creating the ImmunoCluster framework was to support nonspecialist researchers to carry out complex immunophenotyping experiments.
evidence: This describes the motivation for developing ImmunoCluster.

claim: The dawn of 'cytometry big data' and its ever-growing utilization has surpassed the number of experimental parameters that a researcher can feasibly analyze as a collective.
source: The dawn of 'cytometry big data' and its ever-growing utilization has surpassed the number of experimental parameters that a researcher can feasibly analyze as a collective.
evidence: This is an observation about the current state of the field.

claim: ImmunoCluster was designed in collaboration between wet lab and computational biologists.
source: The ImmunoCluster framework was designed in collaboration between wet lab and computational biologists, with the purpose of creating a tool that enables state-of-the-art analysis, yet easy to use in its application.
evidence: This describes the development process of ImmunoCluster.

claim: ImmunoCluster has been built with an emphasis on generalizability and scalability to facilitate a broad use.
source: ImmunoCluster has been built with an emphasis on generalizability and scalability to facilitate a broad use and is an advance over other open-source tools as it provides an integrated framework to uniquely perform a complete computational pipeline on high-dimensional LMC, IMC, and FC data.
evidence: This describes the design philosophy of ImmunoCluster.

claim: ImmunoCluster is an advance over other open-source tools as it provides an integrated framework to uniquely perform a complete computational pipeline on high-dimensional LMC, IMC, and FC data.
source: ImmunoCluster has been built with an emphasis on generalizability and scalability to facilitate a broad use and is an advance over other open-source tools as it provides an integrated framework to uniquely perform a complete computational pipeline on high-dimensional LMC, IMC, and FC data.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of ImmunoCluster over existing tools.

claim: The inclusion of IMC data analysis brings a unique element to the ImmunoCluster framework and differentiates it from other published protocols.
source: The inclusion of IMC data analysis brings a unique element to the ImmunoCluster framework and differentiates it from other published protocols.
evidence: This is a claim about what makes ImmunoCluster unique.

claim: ImmunoCluster can be run on a local desktop/laptop computer with standard configuration.
source: ImmunoCluster can also be run on a local desktop/laptop computer with standard configuration, depending on the number of cells, adaptive downsampling settings and selection of clustering algorithms can usually be run within a day end-to-end (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the computational requirements of ImmunoCluster, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ImmunoCluster can usually be run within a day end-to-end, depending on the number of cells, adaptive downsampling settings and selection of clustering algorithms.
source: ImmunoCluster can also be run on a local desktop/laptop computer with standard configuration, depending on the number of cells, adaptive downsampling settings and selection of clustering algorithms can usually be run within a day end-to-end (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the runtime of ImmunoCluster, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The FlowSOM-based clustering method can be implemented on much larger datasets than PhenoGraph.
source: Whilst the PhenoGraph clustering method does not readily scale, the FlowSOM-based clustering method can be implemented on much larger datasets.
evidence: This is a comparison of clustering methods available in ImmunoCluster.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of samples is the most important stage of the ImmunoCluster framework.
source: Unsupervised clustering (stage 2) of samples is the most important stage of the framework, and its ability to accurately define populations across all samples is critical to all later stages of investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of a particular stage in the workflow.

claim: The number of k clusters to generate (cluster resolution) can significantly affect the ability to identify or determine a change in a biologically relevant population.
source: The number of k clusters to generate (cluster resolution) can significantly affect the ability to identify or determine a change in a biologically relevant population.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation and consideration in using the framework.

claim: Technical inter-sample marker signal variability due to batch effects may impact the ability of unsupervised analysis to reliably detect certain populations if significant batch effects are present.
source: Technical inter-sample marker signal variability due to batch effects may impact the ability of unsupervised analysis to reliably detect certain populations if significant batch effects are present.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the approach.

claim: Sample barcoding is commonly employed in mass cytometry to reduce variability between samples.
source: An approach commonly employed in mass cytometry to overcome this is to use sample barcoding, reducing the variability between each sample, allowing all samples to be exposed to the same antibody mixture (Schulz and Mei, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schulz and Mei, 2019.

claim: CytofRUV is a recently developed package specifically designed for CyTOF dataset batch correction.
source: Statistical methods for batch correction may also be applied; in recent years, a class of methods called remove unwanted variation (RUV) have been developed, and CytofRUV (Trussart et al., 2020) is a recently developed package specifically designed for CyTOF dataset batch correction.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trussart et al., 2020.

claim: Channel spillover still exists in fluorescence-based FC and should be considered when designing antibody panels.
source: Although channel spillover is diminished in mass cytometry, it still exists in fluorescence-based FC and should be considered when designing antibody panels to reduce the effects on introducing cell phenotype artifacts in downstream unsupervised analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about a technical consideration in FC experiments.

claim: In the clinically relevant immune monitoring case study, the ImmunoCluster framework successfully identified 24 phenotypically distinct cell clusters.
source: In our clinically relevant immune monitoring case study setting, the ImmunoCluster framework successfully identified 24 phenotypically distinct cell clusters, and their abundance across all samples, and highlighted differentially represented cells between GvHD and none patients, all of which were consistent with the Hartmann et al. data (Hartmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the case study, supported by citation to Hartmann et al., 2019.

claim: ImmunoCluster highlighted differentially represented cells between GvHD and none patients, consistent with the Hartmann et al. data.
source: In our clinically relevant immune monitoring case study setting, the ImmunoCluster framework successfully identified 24 phenotypically distinct cell clusters, and their abundance across all samples, and highlighted differentially represented cells between GvHD and none patients, all of which were consistent with the Hartmann et al. data (Hartmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the case study, supported by citation to Hartmann et al., 2019.

claim: The publicly available dataset from the Hartmann et al. study was extracted from the FlowRepository.
source: The publicly available dataset from the Hartmann et al. study was extracted for the current study from the FlowRepository (http://flowrepository.org/id/FR-FCM-Z244) (Spidlen et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data source, supported by citation to Spidlen et al., 2012.

claim: Raw FCS files for the LMC dataset were collected on the Helios CyTOF system.
source: Raw FCS files for the LMC dataset that were collected on the Helios CyTOF system (Fluidigm, UK) machine were first normalized using the free CyTOF 6.7 system control software (files can also be concatenated using the same software if necessary).
evidence: This describes the data collection method.

claim: The LMC dataset files were gated to remove beads, doublets, dead cells, and non-CD45+ cells as well as erythrocytes (CD235αβ/CD61+) and neutrophils (CD16+).
source: These files were gated using FlowJo (version 10.5.3) (Becton, Dickinson and Company, UK) to remove beads, doublets, dead cells, and non-CD45+ cells as well as erythrocytes (CD235αβ/CD61+) and neutrophils (CD16+) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), as described by Hartmann et al., 2019, before implementation into the ImmunoCluster framework.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and citation to Hartmann et al., 2019.
